prompt: I would like to outperform the S&P 500 in the next year. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy?
reply:
Here are 10 stock ideas, but first a few caveats that affect how you should use them.

## Caveats

1. **Beating the S&P 500 is hard.** Over 10+ years, roughly 85–90% of professional large-cap fund managers underperform it. Over a single year, the result is close to a coin flip, and you often need luck.
2. **My information stops around May 2026.** I can't see current prices, valuations, or news from the past few months. Check each name before buying.
3. **This isn't personalized advice.** I don't know your finances, taxes, or risk tolerance.
4. **To beat the index, you have to hold something different from it.** Many of these names are already large S&P 500 weights. Buying them outperforms only if they beat the other ~490 companies. The more your portfolio differs from the index, the higher both your upside and your risk of underperforming.

## 10 stocks to research

| # | Stock | Thesis | Key risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Nvidia (NVDA)** | Dominant supplier of AI accelerators, with a strong software moat (CUDA) | Slower AI spending; custom chips from its own customers |
| 2 | **TSMC (TSM)** | Manufactures most leading-edge chips for Nvidia, Apple, AMD and others; not in the S&P 500, so it adds differentiation | Taiwan geopolitical risk |
| 3 | **Broadcom (AVGO)** | Custom AI chips for hyperscalers, AI networking, plus recurring VMware software revenue | Depends on a few large customers; high valuation |
| 4 | **Microsoft (MSFT)** | Azure cloud growth, AI across Office and enterprise software, very durable cash flows | Heavy AI capex may pressure margins |
| 5 | **Alphabet (GOOGL)** | Search cash cow, Google Cloud, in-house TPU chips, Waymo optionality; often cheaper than peers | AI disruption of search; antitrust remedies |
| 6 | **Amazon (AMZN)** | AWS, a fast-growing ad business, and improving retail margins | Consumer slowdown; cloud competition |
| 7 | **Eli Lilly (LLY)** | Leader in GLP-1 obesity and diabetes drugs, with an oral pipeline | Drug pricing pressure; valuation already assumes a lot |
| 8 | **GE Vernova (GEV)** | Gas turbines and grid equipment for rising electricity demand, including data centers | Stock has already risen a lot; execution risk |
| 9 | **Visa (V)** | Takes a cut of global card spending, with very high margins | Regulation of fees; a recession reducing spending |
| 10 | **Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.B)** | Defensive ballast with a large cash pile to use in a downturn | Likely lags in strong bull markets; transition from Buffett to Greg Abel |

## Weaknesses of this list

- **It's concentrated in AI.** About six of these names would fall together if AI spending slows, so they're less diversified than 10 stocks sounds. Berkshire, Visa and Lilly are there partly to offset that.
- **Valuations matter over a one-year horizon.** Some of these may have run up or sold off since my data ends. A great company bought at a high price can still underperform for a year.

## A more practical approach

Many investors use a **core and satellite** setup:
- **Core (70–90%):** a low-cost S&P 500 or total-market index fund, so you never badly trail the market.
- **Satellite (10–30%):** your own stock picks, like the ones above, for a chance to outperform.

Size each stock position so a 50% drop in any one name wouldn't seriously hurt you. Also decide in advance what would make you sell.

If you tell me your risk tolerance and what you already own, I can adjust the list, for example toward more defensive or less tech-heavy names.
